data.topic: The full story behind a prospector's horrifying 1874 ordeal in Colorado's San Juan Mountains — what really happened, beyond what this video tells

read.lede: The record here is a single retelling, not a body of independent investigations: it preserves competing versions of what happened, later physical evidence that cuts both ways, and a legal judgment that Alfred Packer was guilty of voluntary manslaughter rather than proving exactly how each man died. The most unsettling fact is not simply that Packer—the “Colorado Cannibal”—emerged alive after two months in the San Juan Mountains; it is that he emerged with a full belly, other men's possessions, and money he could not explain.

paragraphs.label: The expedition
paragraphs.text: Packer's ordeal began during a larger rush toward Colorado's goldfields. On November 20, 1873, about twenty men left Bingham Canyon, Utah, hoping to reach newly advertised goldfields near Breckenridge. Packer joined them roughly twenty-five miles south of Salt Lake City after offering his services as a guide. He had worked as a guide, hunter, range hand, animal driver and mining laborer, but his reputation was poor. People knew him for getting lost, arguing with clients, stealing, lying and being difficult to trust. He had also enlisted in the Union Army twice, but epilepsy and recurring seizures led to honorable discharges after only a few months each time. Whatever experience Packer possessed, he did not know the route as well as he claimed. He led the party roughly 260 miles to the area outside Montrose, but the journey had already become a winter survival test. Heavy snow obscured the trail, the men lost their way while following a compass, and by January they had run out of food and begun eating horse feed. They were even considering eating the horses when they reached a Ute camp led by Chief Ouray on January 21. The prospectors divided because they feared that waiting would let other gold seekers reach the fields first. Chief Ouray had given the starving men food and shelter and advised them to remain with him until spring. The prospectors were one of many groups racing toward the rumored riches.

paragraphs.label: The crossing
paragraphs.text: The next 120 miles included the San Juan Mountains, and by February the weather had not improved. Ouray reportedly warned that no Ute would attempt the crossing under those conditions because it would mean certain death. One group stayed behind with the horses and wagons, while the other attempted to reach the Los Piños Indian Agency. Ouray advised the travelers to descend to the Gunnison River, follow it, and then turn north toward the agency. Packer insisted on crossing the mountains directly, claiming that route would be faster and that he knew the country. Five men accepted his route. The group that followed the river also suffered badly: its food ran out before the agency, and cowhands eventually found and fed the men at a cattle camp. They reached the agency in May, after the weather improved. Packer's party never arrived together. According to the expedition's leader, the men first traveled on horseback along the river until the animals could go no farther. After arguing with Packer, the leader unloaded their provisions and took the horses back to Ouray's camp. The remaining men had only about fourteen days of food, inadequate clothing, no snowshoes, no flints, almost no matches, and a few rifles, a pistol, a hatchet and knives for a winter crossing.

paragraphs.label: The survivor
paragraphs.text: Packer’s account immediately looked suspicious because his appearance did not match his claim of surviving for months in the wilderness. On April 16, 1874, he appeared at the agency’s mess hall during a fierce snowstorm, wearing rags over his feet instead of shoes, carrying a rifle and a coffee pot, and sporting a long beard. He said the other men had become too exhausted to continue, snow blindness and frostbite had overcome him, and he had been left to fend for himself. He claimed that rabbits, roots and rosebuds had sustained him for months, while his guiding experience had helped him escape. Men previously trapped in the wilderness usually arrived skeletal, but Packer had a bloated face and a well-fed belly. He ate so quickly that he vomited, then went to Saguache, where he spent more than one hundred dollars on whiskey and gambling—about $3,800 in 2023 dollars—and another seventy-eight dollars at a general store. Packer had sold his rifle for only ten dollars, yet seemed never to run out of cash. People also saw him with different wallets, while the rifle and pipe he carried or left behind belonged to other party members. Preston Nutter, who led the men who had taken the river route, said the others would not have abandoned Packer. He immediately questioned how a man who had joined the expedition without money had suddenly acquired cash and their possessions.

paragraphs.label: The accounts and bodies
paragraphs.text: The later evidence led investigators to consider whether Packer had killed the men for their possessions, become trapped by the weather, and then eaten them. Under questioning, Packer first said he had stayed behind by a fire after getting his feet wet and cold, while the others failed to return. When a council gathered to examine his account, two Ute men arrived with pieces of flesh they said came from a human body found on a hill near the agency. Packer reportedly fainted, begged for mercy and changed his story. He was also reported to have said, “It would not be the first time that people had been obliged to eat each other when they were hungry.” In this second version, the oldest man died about ten days into the journey, and the starving survivors ate him and took his rifle. Five days later, another man died, and they ate him, finding $133 in his pockets. A third man died while Packer was away gathering wood. Packer said Shannon Bell then shot the remaining men, carried some of the bodies for food and buried the rest. Two weeks later, Bell allegedly attacked Packer, forcing Packer to shoot him in self-defense. General Charles Adams recorded this account as a sworn statement, but Nutter believed Packer had killed the men himself. Nutter nearly killed Packer during a confrontation, and authorities arrested Packer for manslaughter. Adams's initial search did not find the bodies. In August, however, illustrator John Randolph discovered five decomposing bodies near a tributary of the Gunnison, close to the place Packer had said Bell was left. Randolph sketched the scene and alerted authorities; a team of twenty volunteers later retrieved the remains. The bodies showed violent injuries: two skulls had been struck with a blunt object, Bell had suffered a similar head injury, and someone had deliberately removed the edible portions from the bodies. A later coroner concluded that blows to the head had killed all five while they slept, and that none had defensive wounds. Rags under their feet suggested that they had eaten their shoes, and a trail led to a makeshift shelter.

paragraphs.label: Packer’s final story
paragraphs.text: Before prosecutors could upgrade the case to first-degree murder, Packer escaped from his log-cabin cell with a key, penknife and food that an unknown person had supplied. He stayed away for nine years, using false names in Arkansas and Arizona before turning up in Cheyenne in 1883. General Adams identified Packer and questioned him again. Packer then gave the account he maintained for the rest of his life. He said the party had left Ouray's camp with enough food for one adult for about a week. Within two or three days, a snowstorm forced them toward higher ground, and by the fourth day they had only a pint of flour. For roughly ten more days, they lived on rosebuds and pine gum while following a ridge to avoid deeper snow. They eventually descended to a river and reached a frozen lake, possibly Lake San Cristobal, where they planned to shelter among trees. Packer said Bell had grown furious with the others and increasingly unstable. One morning, Bell sent Packer uphill with a pistol to look for a route across the mountains. Packer returned after a day and found Bell eating meat beside a man's body, while the other three men lay motionless around the fire. Bell allegedly rushed at Packer with a hatchet, so Packer shot him in the stomach and then finished him. Alone, exhausted and starving, Packer said he spent the night surrounded by “the midnight horrors of starvation as well as those of utter isolation.” In another letter, he called it “the greatest wonder” that he returned to a rational condition. The next day, he tried to retrace his route but failed, built a shelter and finally ate the meat Bell had been consuming. He then survived for about sixty more days on the remains of his companions. An avalanche exposed yellow clay, and Packer recognized the area as Slumgullion Pass, whose color reminded settlers of slumgullion stew. He collected meat, searched the dead men's pockets and found the money he later spent in Saguache. Packer had wrapped his feet in cloth because he had eaten his shoes, and he stopped repeatedly to warm them when they began to freeze. He also admitted that, during Adams's earlier search, he had deliberately prevented the party from reaching the bodies because he could not bear to revisit the scene. He later said he escaped because he feared a mob would get past his guards and kill him.

paragraphs.label: Trials and aftermath
paragraphs.text: Packer's final account never settled the central question of what happened to the party, and the surviving evidence still cannot resolve it. At his first trial, prosecution witnesses said he had repeatedly asked how much money the men possessed, behaved dishonestly before the journey, and told contradictory stories afterward. Prosecutors argued that he deliberately led the party onto the dangerous route to obtain their possessions, then invented a survival story to conceal the killings. Packer testified for six hours, admitted eating the men, and insisted that Bell was responsible for every death except Bell's own. A jury convicted him of premeditated murder, theft and other charges and sentenced him to hang. The court overturned that conviction because Colorado had not established the relevant murder statute until after the killings. At a second trial, hunters testified that game—including rabbits and deer—was plentiful even in bad winter conditions. Prosecutors argued that cannibalism therefore reflected choice rather than unavoidable starvation, and that Packer was at minimum criminally negligent for leading the group into the mountains as an incompetent guide. The jury convicted him of voluntary manslaughter, and the court sentenced him to forty years, the maximum eight years per victim and, according to the account, the longest prison sentence then handed down in the United States. Reporter Polly Pry of the Denver Post later recast him as an ex-soldier persecuted by the establishment. Her stories prompted local businesses to organize petitions, helping secure his parole in 1901 after eighteen years. Later forensic examiners generally leaned toward Packer's guilt. They examined marks across Bell's forearms that could indicate defensive wounds inconsistent with Packer's claim that he shot and quickly finished Bell. Yet a revolver found at the site in 1994 was still loaded with three .38-caliber bullets, and those bullets matched lead fragments in Bell's hip. That match gave at least some support to Packer's claim that Bell was shot. The surviving evidence does not validate his story as a whole. It leaves open the possibility that part of the final account was true, while the sequence, motive and extent of Packer's responsibility remain unresolved. After prison, Packer briefly worked as a guard at the Denver Post. He was later described as kind and charitable, moved to Littleton, bought a copper mine, and returned to prospecting. He died in 1907; a rumor says he was vegetarian by then. No decisive evidence distinguishes between a lone survivor who killed only Bell after discovering a massacre and a self-interested guide who killed the party, stole from the dead and constructed a starvation story around whatever fragments of truth remained.

files.title: Alfred Packer’s background
files.body: The video identifies the man as Alfred Packer, also known as the Colorado Cannibal. Alfred was not originally with the party: the group met him south of Salt Lake City, about 25 miles into its journey. Alfred offered to guide them and claimed that he knew the territory between Utah and Brackenridge well. The party accepted him because they thought someone who knew the route would help. In fact, Alfred did not know where he was going, and he had worked as a guide for only a few months. He had a reputation for getting lost, arguing with clients, stealing, and lying, so people who knew him generally did not like or trust him. As a younger man, Alfred served twice in the Union Army during the Civil War, but each enlistment lasted only a few months because he had epilepsy and seizures; he was honorably discharged both times. Afterward, he drove horses and other draft animals across the West, worked as a hunter and a range hand, did odd jobs for mining companies, and briefly tried mining in Colorado. After prison, Alfred seemed to be a changed man. He worked for a while as a guard at the Denver Post, and people described him as kind, modest, and charitable—unlike the grumpy, greedy, and untrustworthy man he had been in the past. Alfred eventually moved to Littleton, where he bought a copper mine and returned to prospecting. The video says he died in 1907 at age 65, and adds that there is a rumor he was a vegetarian when he died.

files.title: The journey to the mountains
files.body:
The group was traveling to the newly found goldfields near Breckenridge, Colorado. After the party left Utah, Alfred guided them as far as just outside Montrose, though the account says he managed this by getting lucky. The journey from Utah to Colorado was made harder by heavy snow, which slowed the wagons and made the trail difficult to follow. The men followed a compass for a while but still got lost, and by January they were completely out of food. They began eating horse feed and even considered eating the horses. The men later described Alfred as greedy, lazy, and constantly fighting with someone.

On January 21, most of the men found the camp of a Native American band of Utes led by Chief Ouray in a valley outside Montrose. Chief Ouray gave the starving men food and shelter and suggested that they stay until the weather improved. The group still had roughly 120 miles and the San Juan Mountains ahead of them. Chief Ouray warned that no Ute would try the journey in those conditions and that it would mean certain death. The men feared that other groups would get the gold before they did, so they decided to leave half the party behind with the horses and wagons until spring and send the other half toward the Los Piños Indian Agency.

Chief Ouray advised them to drop down to the Gunnison River and follow it north to the agency. Alfred insisted that it would be better to cross the mountains directly, said that he knew the area, and claimed that his route would be quicker. Five of the men believed Alfred and chose his plan. The group without Alfred followed the river and suffered brutal cold and food shortages before being rescued by cowhands. Those cowhands fed them and kept them at their cattle camp until spring. In April, when the weather improved, the surviving men reached the agency in May.

The party leader gave a different account of Alfred’s group’s movements. He said they followed the river on horseback until the horses could go no farther. The leader then took the horses back to the Ute camp, leaving the men with limited supplies. The men then likely walked down the river a bit farther and took a path high into the mountains. At the drop-off point, they had only about 14 days of food, inadequate clothes, no snowshoes or flints, and hardly any matches. They had a few rifles, one pistol, a hatchet, and some knives. After the leader turned back, no one heard from the men again until Alfred appeared at the agency months later.

files.title: Packer’s return and suspicions
files.body: Two months later, only one man emerged from the mountains, and he looked weirdly fed instead of emaciated. On April 16, 1874, the source’s account describes a man arriving at the Los Piños Indian Agency with rags on his feet, a long beard, a coffee pot hanging from one side, and a rifle over the other. He begged for help and was identified as Alfred Packer. General Charles Adams had Alfred brought to a table with food, and Alfred ate so fast that he threw up. While drinking whiskey, Alfred told the workers that his companions had become too exhausted to continue, that he had snow blindness and frostbite, and that he had been left behind to fend for himself. Alfred said that for months he had eaten rabbits, roots, and rosebuds before getting out alive. The agency’s workers found it strange that Alfred looked well fed. By May, when Preston Nutter arrived at the agency as the leader of the party that had followed the river, Alfred had already arrived alone and left again; none of the other men had been with him. Alfred later went to Saguache, rented a room and saloon, spent over $100 on drinking and gambling, and spent another $78 in a general store. When he was drinking, Alfred often gave conflicting stories about what had happened. Some people said he seemed to use a different wallet each time he went out and never appeared to run out of cash. Alfred had sold his rifle at the agency for only $10, which did not explain the rest of the money. Preston went to Saguache and became immediately suspicious of Alfred’s story. He told General Adams that the other men would not have left Alfred for dead. Preston said the rifle Alfred sold belonged to an old man in the group and that the pipe Alfred left behind belonged to Shannon Bell. He also pointed out that Alfred had no money when he first joined the group. General Adams sent a man on horseback to bring Alfred in for questioning. When Alfred returned, Adams and his men asked where he got the money, why he had the other men’s belongings, and how he had survived the mountains while appearing well fed. Alfred first claimed that he had stayed by the fire after getting his feet wet and cold while the others went for food. He said that when the others did not return, he assumed they had abandoned him. The source says that, because the account still made no sense to Preston, a council was formed to investigate the matter further.

files.title: The confession
files.body: As the meeting began, two Ute men arrived with pieces of flesh they said came from a human found on a hill near the agency. The account says Alfred panicked, fainted, woke up, begged for mercy, and then, sobbing, gave a different story. Alfred was reportedly heard to say, “It would not be the first time that people had been obliged to eat each other when they were hungry.” He then said that ten days into the journey the party ran out of food. According to Alfred, the oldest man died first, and the others ate him and took his rifle. Five days later, another man died, and the group ate him too; Alfred said they found $133 in that man’s pockets. Alfred said another man later died while he was gathering wood for the fire, and, according to Alfred, the remaining men ate that man as well. Alfred said Shannon Bell then shot the remaining men. He said that he and Shannon carried some of the bodies for food and covered up the rest. Alfred said Shannon later tried to kill him, and that he shot Shannon in self-defense. General Adams wrote down Alfred’s confession and made him sign it as a sworn statement. Preston did not believe Alfred and thought Alfred had killed the others and stolen their belongings. Preston became so angry that he dragged Alfred outside and would have killed him if others had not intervened.

files.title: The bodies and investigation
files.body: The account says Alfred was arrested for manslaughter and locked in a log cabin owned by the sheriff of Saguache. That summer, General Adams took Alfred and some men into the mountains to search for the bodies, but they found nothing. In August, while Alfred was awaiting trial, illustrator John Randolph was traveling over the mountains near Lake City. Near a tributary of the Gunnison River, close to where Alfred had said he left Shannon, John noticed something sticking out of the ground. He found five men in different states of decomposition, and it was clear they had died violently. One man was little more than bones, apparently after animals had gotten to him. Two men had blunt-force injuries to the head, and Shannon Bell had been stripped to the bones except for his hands and feet and also had a blunt head injury. The remains showed a deliberate removal of the edible portions; with the exception of the first man, it did not look as though animals had done it. John made a sketch and reported the scene to authorities in Lake City, after which a team of 20 volunteers recovered the bodies. The coroner concluded that they had all been killed by blows to the head while asleep. None of the bodies had defensive wounds or injuries, and they all had similar skull markings. The bodies had rags under their feet, suggesting they may have eaten the leather from their shoes, and authorities also found a track to a makeshift shelter. These findings led people to speculate that Alfred had killed the men for their possessions, become trapped by weather, and eaten them to survive. Alfred’s charges were expected to be upgraded from manslaughter to first-degree murder, but before that could happen, someone gave him a key, a penknife, and some food so he could escape. The account says that, over the following century, several groups conducted forensic analyses of the remains and compared them with Alfred’s account. Their conclusions have tended to lean toward Alfred being guilty, although some analyses found defensive wounds on some of the bones in the group. One group found marks across Shannon Bell’s forearms, suggesting that Shannon may have defended himself from an attack. In Alfred’s account, however, Shannon was only shot once and then finished quickly. Some evidence also seems to corroborate Alfred’s story: an 1862 Colt revolver found at the murder site in 1994 was still loaded with three .38-caliber bullets, and those bullets matched lead fragments found in Shannon Bell’s hip. That match suggests that at least part of Alfred’s story may have been true.

files.title: The escape and final story
files.body:
The video’s narration says that, after Alfred’s charges were expected to be upgraded from manslaughter to first-degree murder, someone gave him a key, a penknife, and food, although it remains unclear who was responsible. Alfred slipped out of his cell and was not seen for nine years. On March 11, a man came to a shop in Cheyenne, Wyoming, to buy supplies and gave his name as John Schwartze. The shopkeeper thought the man looked familiar and briefly wondered whether he was the same John Schwartze he had known at a Native American camp years earlier. Looking again, he realized the man was actually Alfred Packer. The shopkeeper told the local sheriff that he had spotted a criminal, and Alfred was arrested and taken to Denver. General Adams later confirmed Alfred’s identity and took him away for trial. Adams asked Alfred again what really happened years earlier, and Alfred gave a final story that he more or less stuck to until he died.

In Alfred’s final story, the party left Chief Ouray’s camp with barely enough food for one grown man for a week. After two or three days, a brutal snowstorm hit the party. They reached the base of a mountain and then a deep valley, but the snow on the far side was so deep that they could barely walk. This forced them to move to higher ground, and by day four they had only about a pint of flour left. For the next ten days or so, they lived only on rosebuds and pine gum while following a ridge above the deeper snow. Alfred said several of the men were in rough shape, cried out every night, and prayed to escape alive. The party eventually crossed the main ridge and camped by a river. They followed the stream for a day and reached a frozen lake, possibly Lake San Cristobal. The men decided to cross the lake to reach some trees for shelter. By then, they were exhausted and tensions were rising.

According to Alfred, Shannon Bell was furious with him for getting them lost and angry at the others for acting pathetic. Alfred said Shannon later behaved stranger than usual and may have had a plan to survive, may have been going insane, or both. Shannon told Alfred to scout higher up the mountain for a way across. Alfred took a pistol and went out, but he found only steep slopes and more snow. Alfred admitted to General Adams for the first time that he was only partly a guide: he did not really know what he was doing or that side of the mountains.

When Alfred returned, he found Shannon eating a piece of meat. Alfred saw a dead man near the fire and the other three men lying around it motionless. According to Alfred, Shannon rushed at him with a hatchet, and Alfred shot him in the stomach and then finished him off after he fell. Alfred later described that night as one of the worst of his life and said he was surrounded by “the midnight horrors of starvation as well as those of utter isolation.” Alfred said he felt himself losing his sanity and began to understand what had happened to Shannon. In another letter, Alfred wrote, “The greatest wonder is that I ever returned to a rational condition.”

The next morning, Alfred tried to follow his tracks from the day before but had to turn back because of snow and exhaustion. He built a small shelter from wood and branches, but it did not satisfy his hunger. Alfred decided hunting was not a reliable source of food after the time they had spent there. Alfred said the relief of eating overcame the horror of cannibalism, and he knew what he had to do to survive. He said he then spent two more months in the shelter surviving off the rest of his party. Sixty days later, Alfred saw an avalanche that left yellow clay behind. The yellow clay told him he was in an area known as Slumgullion Pass. The pass was named for its yellow color and for the resemblance early settlers saw to Slumgullion stew.

In early spring, Alfred finally had an idea of where to go and started up the mountain again. Before leaving, Alfred gathered some remaining meat and wrapped it to eat while walking. He also searched the other men’s pockets and found the money he later spent in Saguache. Alfred had already eaten his shoes, so he wrapped his feet in cloth and sometimes stopped because they froze. When his feet froze, he lit a fire to warm them. Near the agency, Alfred ate the last pieces of meat and may have dropped some of it, which the Utes later found.

Alfred also admitted that when he had been with General Adams’ search party a decade earlier, he took the men as far as the mountains opposite the camp and tried to stop them from going farther. Alfred said he wanted to take them farther to show them the truth, but he also did not want to return and remember the horror. He said he escaped and ran from trial because he feared a mob would get past his guard and kill him. He had already nearly been killed by Preston Nutter, and he thought someone would eventually finish the job. After escaping, Alfred went to Arkansas under a fake name and worked on a ranch before moving to Arizona and then to Cheyenne, where he was found.

Alfred’s story eventually reached Polly Pry, a reporter for the Denver Post. She wrote stories about him and portrayed him as a man of the people. She claimed he was an ex-soldier persecuted by the establishment and a man who was in the wrong place at the wrong time. She also claimed he survived horrors that most people could not imagine. She said his sentence was so harsh because of the cannibalism, but that anyone would have done the same in that situation. Over time, Polly Pry’s stories had such an impact that local businesses started arranging petitions for Alfred’s release. The Colorado governor eventually paroled Alfred in 1901, after he had served 18 years of his sentence.

files.title: The trial and sentence
files.body:
At trial, several parts of Alfred’s story were questioned, and people became convinced that the crime had been deliberate and premeditated. The prosecution argued that Alfred had intentionally led the men astray so he could steal their possessions by any means necessary. Witnesses testified about his behavior after he reached Saguache and about the conflicting accounts he gave of what had happened. When Alfred testified, he spoke for six hours, admitted eating the other men, and swore that he had killed only Shannon, while Shannon was responsible for everything else. The jury found Alfred guilty of premeditated murder, theft, and several other charges, and he was sentenced to be hanged.

Alfred’s lawyers found a technicality before the hanging could happen. Colorado became a state in 1876, and before statehood Colorado Territory did not have a statute under which Alfred could be tried for murder. Colorado State established the specific laws for the crime only after the crime had already taken place. Because of that legal issue, Alfred’s murder conviction was overturned, and he had to be retried for manslaughter instead of murder.

In the new trial, Alfred pleaded not guilty and stuck to his story. The prosecution brought in hunters who said there was plenty of food in the area even during a bad winter. They testified that game, rabbits, deer, and other food would have been easy to hunt, even for someone as inexperienced as Alfred. The prosecution argued that the cannibalism therefore had to have been by choice, because food would have been available. When Alfred took the stand, his testimony lasted six hours and did not help his case. It was also argued that Alfred might not have been a malicious monster, but that he had still led the group astray by hiking the more dangerous route in winter under the guise of being a guide. The prosecution said that, in the best case, Alfred was extremely negligent.

Alfred was eventually found guilty of voluntary manslaughter and received 40 years in prison, the maximum of eight years per man. At the time, that was the longest prison sentence handed down in US history. After he was imprisoned, Alfred wrote to anyone he could, saying that the sentence was unjust, that he had killed only Shannon, and that the jury was full of biased and prejudiced people.

# The full story behind a prospector's horrifying 1874 ordeal in Colorado's San Juan Mountains — what really happened, beyond what this video tells

1 sources · 5,100 raw words read · quotes verified 100% · 2026-08-30

## 1. The Read

The record here is a single retelling, not a body of independent investigations: it preserves competing versions of what happened, later physical evidence that cuts both ways, and a legal judgment that Alfred Packer was guilty of voluntary manslaughter rather than proving exactly how each man died. The most unsettling fact is not simply that Packer—the “Colorado Cannibal”—emerged alive after two months in the San Juan Mountains; it is that he emerged with a full belly, other men's possessions, and money he could not explain.

**The expedition:** Packer's ordeal began during a larger rush toward Colorado's goldfields. On November 20, 1873, about twenty men left Bingham Canyon, Utah, hoping to reach newly advertised goldfields near Breckenridge. Packer joined them roughly twenty-five miles south of Salt Lake City after offering his services as a guide. He had worked as a guide, hunter, range hand, animal driver and mining laborer, but his reputation was poor. People knew him for getting lost, arguing with clients, stealing, lying and being difficult to trust. He had also enlisted in the Union Army twice, but epilepsy and recurring seizures led to honorable discharges after only a few months each time. Whatever experience Packer possessed, he did not know the route as well as he claimed. He led the party roughly 260 miles to the area outside Montrose, but the journey had already become a winter survival test. Heavy snow obscured the trail, the men lost their way while following a compass, and by January they had run out of food and begun eating horse feed. They were even considering eating the horses when they reached a Ute camp led by Chief Ouray on January 21. The prospectors divided because they feared that waiting would let other gold seekers reach the fields first. Chief Ouray had given the starving men food and shelter and advised them to remain with him until spring. The prospectors were one of many groups racing toward the rumored riches.

**The crossing:** The next 120 miles included the San Juan Mountains, and by February the weather had not improved. Ouray reportedly warned that no Ute would attempt the crossing under those conditions because it would mean certain death. One group stayed behind with the horses and wagons, while the other attempted to reach the Los Piños Indian Agency. Ouray advised the travelers to descend to the Gunnison River, follow it, and then turn north toward the agency. Packer insisted on crossing the mountains directly, claiming that route would be faster and that he knew the country. Five men accepted his route. The group that followed the river also suffered badly: its food ran out before the agency, and cowhands eventually found and fed the men at a cattle camp. They reached the agency in May, after the weather improved. Packer's party never arrived together. According to the expedition's leader, the men first traveled on horseback along the river until the animals could go no farther. After arguing with Packer, the leader unloaded their provisions and took the horses back to Ouray's camp. The remaining men had only about fourteen days of food, inadequate clothing, no snowshoes, no flints, almost no matches, and a few rifles, a pistol, a hatchet and knives for a winter crossing.

**The survivor:** Packer’s account immediately looked suspicious because his appearance did not match his claim of surviving for months in the wilderness. On April 16, 1874, he appeared at the agency’s mess hall during a fierce snowstorm, wearing rags over his feet instead of shoes, carrying a rifle and a coffee pot, and sporting a long beard. He said the other men had become too exhausted to continue, snow blindness and frostbite had overcome him, and he had been left to fend for himself. He claimed that rabbits, roots and rosebuds had sustained him for months, while his guiding experience had helped him escape. Men previously trapped in the wilderness usually arrived skeletal, but Packer had a bloated face and a well-fed belly. He ate so quickly that he vomited, then went to Saguache, where he spent more than one hundred dollars on whiskey and gambling—about $3,800 in 2023 dollars—and another seventy-eight dollars at a general store. Packer had sold his rifle for only ten dollars, yet seemed never to run out of cash. People also saw him with different wallets, while the rifle and pipe he carried or left behind belonged to other party members. Preston Nutter, who led the men who had taken the river route, said the others would not have abandoned Packer. He immediately questioned how a man who had joined the expedition without money had suddenly acquired cash and their possessions.

**The accounts and bodies:** The later evidence led investigators to consider whether Packer had killed the men for their possessions, become trapped by the weather, and then eaten them. Under questioning, Packer first said he had stayed behind by a fire after getting his feet wet and cold, while the others failed to return. When a council gathered to examine his account, two Ute men arrived with pieces of flesh they said came from a human body found on a hill near the agency. Packer reportedly fainted, begged for mercy and changed his story. He was also reported to have said, “It would not be the first time that people had been obliged to eat each other when they were hungry.” In this second version, the oldest man died about ten days into the journey, and the starving survivors ate him and took his rifle. Five days later, another man died, and they ate him, finding $133 in his pockets. A third man died while Packer was away gathering wood. Packer said Shannon Bell then shot the remaining men, carried some of the bodies for food and buried the rest. Two weeks later, Bell allegedly attacked Packer, forcing Packer to shoot him in self-defense. General Charles Adams recorded this account as a sworn statement, but Nutter believed Packer had killed the men himself. Nutter nearly killed Packer during a confrontation, and authorities arrested Packer for manslaughter. Adams's initial search did not find the bodies. In August, however, illustrator John Randolph discovered five decomposing bodies near a tributary of the Gunnison, close to the place Packer had said Bell was left. Randolph sketched the scene and alerted authorities; a team of twenty volunteers later retrieved the remains. The bodies showed violent injuries: two skulls had been struck with a blunt object, Bell had suffered a similar head injury, and someone had deliberately removed the edible portions from the bodies. A later coroner concluded that blows to the head had killed all five while they slept, and that none had defensive wounds. Rags under their feet suggested that they had eaten their shoes, and a trail led to a makeshift shelter.

**Packer’s final story:** Before prosecutors could upgrade the case to first-degree murder, Packer escaped from his log-cabin cell with a key, penknife and food that an unknown person had supplied. He stayed away for nine years, using false names in Arkansas and Arizona before turning up in Cheyenne in 1883. General Adams identified Packer and questioned him again. Packer then gave the account he maintained for the rest of his life. He said the party had left Ouray's camp with enough food for one adult for about a week. Within two or three days, a snowstorm forced them toward higher ground, and by the fourth day they had only a pint of flour. For roughly ten more days, they lived on rosebuds and pine gum while following a ridge to avoid deeper snow. They eventually descended to a river and reached a frozen lake, possibly Lake San Cristobal, where they planned to shelter among trees. Packer said Bell had grown furious with the others and increasingly unstable. One morning, Bell sent Packer uphill with a pistol to look for a route across the mountains. Packer returned after a day and found Bell eating meat beside a man's body, while the other three men lay motionless around the fire. Bell allegedly rushed at Packer with a hatchet, so Packer shot him in the stomach and then finished him. Alone, exhausted and starving, Packer said he spent the night surrounded by “the midnight horrors of starvation as well as those of utter isolation.” In another letter, he called it “the greatest wonder” that he returned to a rational condition. The next day, he tried to retrace his route but failed, built a shelter and finally ate the meat Bell had been consuming. He then survived for about sixty more days on the remains of his companions. An avalanche exposed yellow clay, and Packer recognized the area as Slumgullion Pass, whose color reminded settlers of slumgullion stew. He collected meat, searched the dead men's pockets and found the money he later spent in Saguache. Packer had wrapped his feet in cloth because he had eaten his shoes, and he stopped repeatedly to warm them when they began to freeze. He also admitted that, during Adams's earlier search, he had deliberately prevented the party from reaching the bodies because he could not bear to revisit the scene. He later said he escaped because he feared a mob would get past his guards and kill him.

**Trials and aftermath:** Packer's final account never settled the central question of what happened to the party, and the surviving evidence still cannot resolve it. At his first trial, prosecution witnesses said he had repeatedly asked how much money the men possessed, behaved dishonestly before the journey, and told contradictory stories afterward. Prosecutors argued that he deliberately led the party onto the dangerous route to obtain their possessions, then invented a survival story to conceal the killings. Packer testified for six hours, admitted eating the men, and insisted that Bell was responsible for every death except Bell's own. A jury convicted him of premeditated murder, theft and other charges and sentenced him to hang. The court overturned that conviction because Colorado had not established the relevant murder statute until after the killings. At a second trial, hunters testified that game—including rabbits and deer—was plentiful even in bad winter conditions. Prosecutors argued that cannibalism therefore reflected choice rather than unavoidable starvation, and that Packer was at minimum criminally negligent for leading the group into the mountains as an incompetent guide. The jury convicted him of voluntary manslaughter, and the court sentenced him to forty years, the maximum eight years per victim and, according to the account, the longest prison sentence then handed down in the United States. Reporter Polly Pry of the Denver Post later recast him as an ex-soldier persecuted by the establishment. Her stories prompted local businesses to organize petitions, helping secure his parole in 1901 after eighteen years. Later forensic examiners generally leaned toward Packer's guilt. They examined marks across Bell's forearms that could indicate defensive wounds inconsistent with Packer's claim that he shot and quickly finished Bell. Yet a revolver found at the site in 1994 was still loaded with three .38-caliber bullets, and those bullets matched lead fragments in Bell's hip. That match gave at least some support to Packer's claim that Bell was shot. The surviving evidence does not validate his story as a whole. It leaves open the possibility that part of the final account was true, while the sequence, motive and extent of Packer's responsibility remain unresolved. After prison, Packer briefly worked as a guard at the Denver Post. He was later described as kind and charitable, moved to Littleton, bought a copper mine, and returned to prospecting. He died in 1907; a rumor says he was vegetarian by then. No decisive evidence distinguishes between a lone survivor who killed only Bell after discovering a massacre and a self-interested guide who killed the party, stole from the dead and constructed a starvation story around whatever fragments of truth remained.

## 2. The Players

**Denver Post** — Newspaper employing Polly Pry as a reporter and Alfred as a guard

The Denver Post recurs through its connection to the case’s reporting and Alfred’s work history. Polly Pry reported on the events, while Alfred worked at the paper as a guard for a time. It is also the destination to which Alfred was taken after a shopkeeper told the local sheriff he had spotted a criminal.

**Gunnison River** — River route followed by the party searching for the agency

Chief Ouray advised the group to descend to the Gunnison River and follow it north to the agency. The men who traveled without Alfred followed the river through brutal cold and food shortages before cowhands rescued them; the party leader said Alfred’s group followed it on horseback until the horses could go no farther. The river also recurs near the location where John Randolph found five violently killed men.

**Preston Nutter** — Leader of the party that followed the Gunnison River and accuser of Alfred

Preston Nutter arrived at the agency in May as leader of the group that had followed the river, then went to Saguache and became immediately suspicious of Alfred’s story. He told General Adams that the others would not have left Alfred for dead, identified the rifle Alfred sold as belonging to an old man in the group, and said the pipe Alfred left behind belonged to Shannon Bell. Preston also noted that Alfred had no money when he joined the group and concluded that Alfred had killed the others and stolen their belongings. He became so angry that he dragged Alfred outside and nearly killed him before others intervened.

**John Randolph** — Illustrator who discovered and reported the remains of five men near the Gunnison River

In August, while Alfred awaited trial, John Randolph was traveling over the mountains near Lake City. Near a tributary of the Gunnison River, close to where Alfred said he had left Shannon, John saw something sticking out of the ground and found five men in different states of decomposition; their violent deaths were apparent. He made a sketch and reported the scene to authorities in Lake City.

The account says Alfred was arrested for manslaughter and locked in a log cabin owned by the sheriff of Saguache. He found five men in different states of decomposition, and it was clear they had died violently. One man was little more than bones, apparently after animals had gotten to him. Two men had blunt-force injuries to the head, and Shannon Bell had been stripped to the bones except for his hands and feet and also had a blunt head injury. The remains showed a deliberate removal of the edible portions; with the exception of the first man, it did not look as though animals had done it. John made a sketch and reported the scene to authorities in Lake City, after which a team of 20 volunteers recovered the bodies. The coroner concluded that they had all been killed by blows to the head while asleep. None of the bodies had defensive wounds or injuries, and they all had similar skull markings. ### The escape and final story `single source`

The video’s narration says that, after Alfred’s charges were expected to be upgraded from manslaughter to first-degree murder, someone gave him a key, a penknife, and food, although it remains unclear who was responsible. Alfred slipped out of his cell and was not seen for nine years. On March 11, a man came to a shop in Cheyenne, Wyoming, to buy supplies and gave his name as John Schwartze. The shopkeeper thought the man looked familiar and briefly wondered whether he was the same John Schwartze he had known at a Native American camp years earlier. Looking again, he realized the man was actually Alfred Packer. The shopkeeper told the local sheriff that he had spotted a criminal, and Alfred was arrested and taken to Denver. General Adams later confirmed Alfred’s identity and took him away for trial. Adams asked Alfred again what really happened years earlier, and Alfred gave a final story that he more or less stuck to until he died.

In Alfred’s final story, the party left Chief Ouray’s camp with barely enough food for one grown man for a week. After two or three days, a brutal snowstorm hit the party. They reached the base of a mountain and then a deep valley, but the snow on the far side was so deep that they could barely walk. This forced them to move to higher ground, and by day four they had only about a pint of flour left. For the next ten days or so, they lived only on rosebuds and pine gum while following a ridge above the deeper snow. Alfred said several of the men were in rough shape, cried out every night, and prayed to escape alive. The party eventually crossed the main ridge and camped by a river. They followed the stream for a day and reached a frozen lake, possibly Lake San Cristobal. The men decided to cross the lake to reach some trees for shelter. By then, they were exhausted and tensions were rising.

According to Alfred, Shannon Bell was furious with him for getting them lost and angry at the others for acting pathetic. Alfred said Shannon later behaved stranger than usual and may have had a plan to survive, may have been going insane, or both. Shannon told Alfred to scout higher up the mountain for a way across. Alfred took a pistol and went out, but he found only steep slopes and more snow. Alfred admitted to General Adams for the first time that he was only partly a guide: he did not really know what he was doing or that side of the mountains.

When Alfred returned, he found Shannon eating a piece of meat. Alfred saw a dead man near the fire and the other three men lying around it motionless. According to Alfred, Shannon rushed at him with a hatchet, and Alfred shot him in the stomach and then finished him off after he fell. Alfred later described that night as one of the worst of his life and said he was surrounded by “the midnight horrors of starvation as well as those of utter isolation.” Alfred said he felt himself losing his sanity and began to understand what had happened to Shannon. In another letter, Alfred wrote, “The greatest wonder is that I ever returned to a rational condition.”

The next morning, Alfred tried to follow his tracks from the day before but had to turn back because of snow and exhaustion. He built a small shelter from wood and branches, but it did not satisfy his hunger. Alfred decided hunting was not a reliable source of food after the time they had spent there. Alfred said the relief of eating overcame the horror of cannibalism, and he knew what he had to do to survive. He said he then spent two more months in the shelter surviving off the rest of his party. Sixty days later, Alfred saw an avalanche that left yellow clay behind. The yellow clay told him he was in an area known as Slumgullion Pass. The pass was named for its yellow color and for the resemblance early settlers saw to Slumgullion stew.

In early spring, Alfred finally had an idea of where to go and started up the mountain again. Before leaving, Alfred gathered some remaining meat and wrapped it to eat while walking. He also searched the other men’s pockets and found the money he later spent in Saguache. Alfred had already eaten his shoes, so he wrapped his feet in cloth and sometimes stopped because they froze. When his feet froze, he lit a fire to warm them. Near the agency, Alfred ate the last pieces of meat and may have dropped some of it, which the Utes later found.

Alfred also admitted that when he had been with General Adams’ search party a decade earlier, he took the men as far as the mountains opposite the camp and tried to stop them from going farther. Alfred said he wanted to take them farther to show them the truth, but he also did not want to return and remember the horror. He said he escaped and ran from trial because he feared a mob would get past his guard and kill him. He had already nearly been killed by Preston Nutter, and he thought someone would eventually finish the job. After escaping, Alfred went to Arkansas under a fake name and worked on a ranch before moving to Arizona and then to Cheyenne, where he was found.

Alfred’s story eventually reached Polly Pry, a reporter for the Denver Post. She wrote stories about him and portrayed him as a man of the people. She claimed he was an ex-soldier persecuted by the establishment and a man who was in the wrong place at the wrong time. She also claimed he survived horrors that most people could not imagine. She said his sentence was so harsh because of the cannibalism, but that anyone would have done the same in that situation. Over time, Polly Pry’s stories had such an impact that local businesses started arranging petitions for Alfred’s release. The Colorado governor eventually paroled Alfred in 1901, after he had served 18 years of his sentence.

### The trial and sentence `single source`

At trial, several parts of Alfred’s story were questioned, and people became convinced that the crime had been deliberate and premeditated. The prosecution argued that Alfred had intentionally led the men astray so he could steal their possessions by any means necessary. Witnesses testified about his behavior after he reached Saguache and about the conflicting accounts he gave of what had happened. When Alfred testified, he spoke for six hours, admitted eating the other men, and swore that he had killed only Shannon, while Shannon was responsible for everything else. The jury found Alfred guilty of premeditated murder, theft, and several other charges, and he was sentenced to be hanged.

Alfred’s lawyers found a technicality before the hanging could happen. Colorado became a state in 1876, and before statehood Colorado Territory did not have a statute under which Alfred could be tried for murder. Colorado State established the specific laws for the crime only after the crime had already taken place. Because of that legal issue, Alfred’s murder conviction was overturned, and he had to be retried for manslaughter instead of murder.

In the new trial, Alfred pleaded not guilty and stuck to his story. The prosecution brought in hunters who said there was plenty of food in the area even during a bad winter. They testified that game, rabbits, deer, and other food would have been easy to hunt, even for someone as inexperienced as Alfred. The prosecution argued that the cannibalism therefore had to have been by choice, because food would have been available. When Alfred took the stand, his testimony lasted six hours and did not help his case. It was also argued that Alfred might not have been a malicious monster, but that he had still led the group astray by hiking the more dangerous route in winter under the guise of being a guide. The prosecution said that, in the best case, Alfred was extremely negligent.

Alfred was eventually found guilty of voluntary manslaughter and received 40 years in prison, the maximum of eight years per man. At the time, that was the longest prison sentence handed down in US history. After he was imprisoned, Alfred wrote to anyone he could, saying that the sentence was unjust, that he had killed only Shannon, and that the jury was full of biased and prejudiced people.

The full story behind a prospector's horrifying 1874 ordeal in Colorado's San Juan Mountains — what really happened, beyond what this video tells

SECTION 1

The Read

The record here is a single retelling, not a body of independent investigations: it preserves competing versions of what happened, later physical evidence that cuts both ways, and a legal judgment that Alfred Packer was guilty of voluntary manslaughter rather than proving exactly how each man died. The most unsettling fact is not simply that Packer—the “Colorado Cannibal”—emerged alive after two months in the San Juan Mountains; it is that he emerged with a full belly, other men's possessions, and money he could not explain.

The expedition: Packer's ordeal began during a larger rush toward Colorado's goldfields. On November 20, 1873, about twenty men left Bingham Canyon, Utah, hoping to reach newly advertised goldfields near Breckenridge. Packer joined them roughly twenty-five miles south of Salt Lake City after offering his services as a guide. He had worked as a guide, hunter, range hand, animal driver and mining laborer, but his reputation was poor. People knew him for getting lost, arguing with clients, stealing, lying and being difficult to trust. He had also enlisted in the Union Army twice, but epilepsy and recurring seizures led to honorable discharges after only a few months each time. Whatever experience Packer possessed, he did not know the route as well as he claimed. He led the party roughly 260 miles to the area outside Montrose, but the journey had already become a winter survival test. Heavy snow obscured the trail, the men lost their way while following a compass, and by January they had run out of food and begun eating horse feed. They were even considering eating the horses when they reached a Ute camp led by Chief Ouray on January 21. The prospectors divided because they feared that waiting would let other gold seekers reach the fields first. Chief Ouray had given the starving men food and shelter and advised them to remain with him until spring. The prospectors were one of many groups racing toward the rumored riches.

The crossing: The next 120 miles included the San Juan Mountains, and by February the weather had not improved. Ouray reportedly warned that no Ute would attempt the crossing under those conditions because it would mean certain death. One group stayed behind with the horses and wagons, while the other attempted to reach the Los Piños Indian Agency. Ouray advised the travelers to descend to the Gunnison River, follow it, and then turn north toward the agency. Packer insisted on crossing the mountains directly, claiming that route would be faster and that he knew the country. Five men accepted his route. The group that followed the river also suffered badly: its food ran out before the agency, and cowhands eventually found and fed the men at a cattle camp. They reached the agency in May, after the weather improved. Packer's party never arrived together. According to the expedition's leader, the men first traveled on horseback along the river until the animals could go no farther. After arguing with Packer, the leader unloaded their provisions and took the horses back to Ouray's camp. The remaining men had only about fourteen days of food, inadequate clothing, no snowshoes, no flints, almost no matches, and a few rifles, a pistol, a hatchet and knives for a winter crossing.

The survivor: Packer’s account immediately looked suspicious because his appearance did not match his claim of surviving for months in the wilderness. On April 16, 1874, he appeared at the agency’s mess hall during a fierce snowstorm, wearing rags over his feet instead of shoes, carrying a rifle and a coffee pot, and sporting a long beard. He said the other men had become too exhausted to continue, snow blindness and frostbite had overcome him, and he had been left to fend for himself. He claimed that rabbits, roots and rosebuds had sustained him for months, while his guiding experience had helped him escape. Men previously trapped in the wilderness usually arrived skeletal, but Packer had a bloated face and a well-fed belly. He ate so quickly that he vomited, then went to Saguache, where he spent more than one hundred dollars on whiskey and gambling—about $3,800 in 2023 dollars—and another seventy-eight dollars at a general store. Packer had sold his rifle for only ten dollars, yet seemed never to run out of cash. People also saw him with different wallets, while the rifle and pipe he carried or left behind belonged to other party members. Preston Nutter, who led the men who had taken the river route, said the others would not have abandoned Packer. He immediately questioned how a man who had joined the expedition without money had suddenly acquired cash and their possessions.

The accounts and bodies: The later evidence led investigators to consider whether Packer had killed the men for their possessions, become trapped by the weather, and then eaten them. Under questioning, Packer first said he had stayed behind by a fire after getting his feet wet and cold, while the others failed to return. When a council gathered to examine his account, two Ute men arrived with pieces of flesh they said came from a human body found on a hill near the agency. Packer reportedly fainted, begged for mercy and changed his story. He was also reported to have said, “It would not be the first time that people had been obliged to eat each other when they were hungry.” In this second version, the oldest man died about ten days into the journey, and the starving survivors ate him and took his rifle. Five days later, another man died, and they ate him, finding $133 in his pockets. A third man died while Packer was away gathering wood. Packer said Shannon Bell then shot the remaining men, carried some of the bodies for food and buried the rest. Two weeks later, Bell allegedly attacked Packer, forcing Packer to shoot him in self-defense. General Charles Adams recorded this account as a sworn statement, but Nutter believed Packer had killed the men himself. Nutter nearly killed Packer during a confrontation, and authorities arrested Packer for manslaughter. Adams's initial search did not find the bodies. In August, however, illustrator John Randolph discovered five decomposing bodies near a tributary of the Gunnison, close to the place Packer had said Bell was left. Randolph sketched the scene and alerted authorities; a team of twenty volunteers later retrieved the remains. The bodies showed violent injuries: two skulls had been struck with a blunt object, Bell had suffered a similar head injury, and someone had deliberately removed the edible portions from the bodies. A later coroner concluded that blows to the head had killed all five while they slept, and that none had defensive wounds. Rags under their feet suggested that they had eaten their shoes, and a trail led to a makeshift shelter.

Packer’s final story: Before prosecutors could upgrade the case to first-degree murder, Packer escaped from his log-cabin cell with a key, penknife and food that an unknown person had supplied. He stayed away for nine years, using false names in Arkansas and Arizona before turning up in Cheyenne in 1883. General Adams identified Packer and questioned him again. Packer then gave the account he maintained for the rest of his life. He said the party had left Ouray's camp with enough food for one adult for about a week. Within two or three days, a snowstorm forced them toward higher ground, and by the fourth day they had only a pint of flour. For roughly ten more days, they lived on rosebuds and pine gum while following a ridge to avoid deeper snow. They eventually descended to a river and reached a frozen lake, possibly Lake San Cristobal, where they planned to shelter among trees. Packer said Bell had grown furious with the others and increasingly unstable. One morning, Bell sent Packer uphill with a pistol to look for a route across the mountains. Packer returned after a day and found Bell eating meat beside a man's body, while the other three men lay motionless around the fire. Bell allegedly rushed at Packer with a hatchet, so Packer shot him in the stomach and then finished him. Alone, exhausted and starving, Packer said he spent the night surrounded by “the midnight horrors of starvation as well as those of utter isolation.” In another letter, he called it “the greatest wonder” that he returned to a rational condition. The next day, he tried to retrace his route but failed, built a shelter and finally ate the meat Bell had been consuming. He then survived for about sixty more days on the remains of his companions. An avalanche exposed yellow clay, and Packer recognized the area as Slumgullion Pass, whose color reminded settlers of slumgullion stew. He collected meat, searched the dead men's pockets and found the money he later spent in Saguache. Packer had wrapped his feet in cloth because he had eaten his shoes, and he stopped repeatedly to warm them when they began to freeze. He also admitted that, during Adams's earlier search, he had deliberately prevented the party from reaching the bodies because he could not bear to revisit the scene. He later said he escaped because he feared a mob would get past his guards and kill him.

Trials and aftermath: Packer's final account never settled the central question of what happened to the party, and the surviving evidence still cannot resolve it. At his first trial, prosecution witnesses said he had repeatedly asked how much money the men possessed, behaved dishonestly before the journey, and told contradictory stories afterward. Prosecutors argued that he deliberately led the party onto the dangerous route to obtain their possessions, then invented a survival story to conceal the killings. Packer testified for six hours, admitted eating the men, and insisted that Bell was responsible for every death except Bell's own. A jury convicted him of premeditated murder, theft and other charges and sentenced him to hang. The court overturned that conviction because Colorado had not established the relevant murder statute until after the killings. At a second trial, hunters testified that game—including rabbits and deer—was plentiful even in bad winter conditions. Prosecutors argued that cannibalism therefore reflected choice rather than unavoidable starvation, and that Packer was at minimum criminally negligent for leading the group into the mountains as an incompetent guide. The jury convicted him of voluntary manslaughter, and the court sentenced him to forty years, the maximum eight years per victim and, according to the account, the longest prison sentence then handed down in the United States. Reporter Polly Pry of the Denver Post later recast him as an ex-soldier persecuted by the establishment. Her stories prompted local businesses to organize petitions, helping secure his parole in 1901 after eighteen years. Later forensic examiners generally leaned toward Packer's guilt. They examined marks across Bell's forearms that could indicate defensive wounds inconsistent with Packer's claim that he shot and quickly finished Bell. Yet a revolver found at the site in 1994 was still loaded with three .38-caliber bullets, and those bullets matched lead fragments in Bell's hip. That match gave at least some support to Packer's claim that Bell was shot. The surviving evidence does not validate his story as a whole. It leaves open the possibility that part of the final account was true, while the sequence, motive and extent of Packer's responsibility remain unresolved. After prison, Packer briefly worked as a guard at the Denver Post. He was later described as kind and charitable, moved to Littleton, bought a copper mine, and returned to prospecting. He died in 1907; a rumor says he was vegetarian by then. No decisive evidence distinguishes between a lone survivor who killed only Bell after discovering a massacre and a self-interested guide who killed the party, stole from the dead and constructed a starvation story around whatever fragments of truth remained.

SECTION 2

The Players

Denver PostNewspaper employing Polly Pry as a reporter and Alfred as a guard

The Denver Post recurs through its connection to the case’s reporting and Alfred’s work history. Polly Pry reported on the events, while Alfred worked at the paper as a guard for a time. It is also the destination to which Alfred was taken after a shopkeeper told the local sheriff he had spotted a criminal.

Gunnison RiverRiver route followed by the party searching for the agency

Chief Ouray advised the group to descend to the Gunnison River and follow it north to the agency. The men who traveled without Alfred followed the river through brutal cold and food shortages before cowhands rescued them; the party leader said Alfred’s group followed it on horseback until the horses could go no farther. The river also recurs near the location where John Randolph found five violently killed men.

Preston NutterLeader of the party that followed the Gunnison River and accuser of Alfred

Preston Nutter arrived at the agency in May as leader of the group that had followed the river, then went to Saguache and became immediately suspicious of Alfred’s story. He told General Adams that the others would not have left Alfred for dead, identified the rifle Alfred sold as belonging to an old man in the group, and said the pipe Alfred left behind belonged to Shannon Bell. Preston also noted that Alfred had no money when he joined the group and concluded that Alfred had killed the others and stolen their belongings. He became so angry that he dragged Alfred outside and nearly killed him before others intervened.

John RandolphIllustrator who discovered and reported the remains of five men near the Gunnison River

In August, while Alfred awaited trial, John Randolph was traveling over the mountains near Lake City. Near a tributary of the Gunnison River, close to where Alfred said he had left Shannon, John saw something sticking out of the ground and found five men in different states of decomposition; their violent deaths were apparent. He made a sketch and reported the scene to authorities in Lake City.

The Files

File: Alfred Packer’s background

single source

The video identifies the man as Alfred Packer, also known as the Colorado Cannibal. Alfred was not originally with the party: the group met him south of Salt Lake City, about 25 miles into its journey. Alfred offered to guide them and claimed that he knew the territory between Utah and Brackenridge well. The party accepted him because they thought someone who knew the route would help. In fact, Alfred did not know where he was going, and he had worked as a guide for only a few months. He had a reputation for getting lost, arguing with clients, stealing, and lying, so people who knew him generally did not like or trust him. As a younger man, Alfred served twice in the Union Army during the Civil War, but each enlistment lasted only a few months because he had epilepsy and seizures; he was honorably discharged both times. Afterward, he drove horses and other draft animals across the West, worked as a hunter and a range hand, did odd jobs for mining companies, and briefly tried mining in Colorado. After prison, Alfred seemed to be a changed man. He worked for a while as a guard at the Denver Post, and people described him as kind, modest, and charitable—unlike the grumpy, greedy, and untrustworthy man he had been in the past. Alfred eventually moved to Littleton, where he bought a copper mine and returned to prospecting. The video says he died in 1907 at age 65, and adds that there is a rumor he was a vegetarian when he died.

File: The journey to the mountains

single source

The group was traveling to the newly found goldfields near Breckenridge, Colorado. After the party left Utah, Alfred guided them as far as just outside Montrose, though the account says he managed this by getting lucky. The journey from Utah to Colorado was made harder by heavy snow, which slowed the wagons and made the trail difficult to follow. The men followed a compass for a while but still got lost, and by January they were completely out of food. They began eating horse feed and even considered eating the horses. The men later described Alfred as greedy, lazy, and constantly fighting with someone.

On January 21, most of the men found the camp of a Native American band of Utes led by Chief Ouray in a valley outside Montrose. Chief Ouray gave the starving men food and shelter and suggested that they stay until the weather improved. The group still had roughly 120 miles and the San Juan Mountains ahead of them. Chief Ouray warned that no Ute would try the journey in those conditions and that it would mean certain death. The men feared that other groups would get the gold before they did, so they decided to leave half the party behind with the horses and wagons until spring and send the other half toward the Los Piños Indian Agency.

Chief Ouray advised them to drop down to the Gunnison River and follow it north to the agency. Alfred insisted that it would be better to cross the mountains directly, said that he knew the area, and claimed that his route would be quicker. Five of the men believed Alfred and chose his plan. The group without Alfred followed the river and suffered brutal cold and food shortages before being rescued by cowhands. Those cowhands fed them and kept them at their cattle camp until spring. In April, when the weather improved, the surviving men reached the agency in May.

The party leader gave a different account of Alfred’s group’s movements. He said they followed the river on horseback until the horses could go no farther. The leader then took the horses back to the Ute camp, leaving the men with limited supplies. The men then likely walked down the river a bit farther and took a path high into the mountains. At the drop-off point, they had only about 14 days of food, inadequate clothes, no snowshoes or flints, and hardly any matches. They had a few rifles, one pistol, a hatchet, and some knives. After the leader turned back, no one heard from the men again until Alfred appeared at the agency months later.

File: Packer’s return and suspicions

single source

Two months later, only one man emerged from the mountains, and he looked weirdly fed instead of emaciated. On April 16, 1874, the source’s account describes a man arriving at the Los Piños Indian Agency with rags on his feet, a long beard, a coffee pot hanging from one side, and a rifle over the other. He begged for help and was identified as Alfred Packer. General Charles Adams had Alfred brought to a table with food, and Alfred ate so fast that he threw up. While drinking whiskey, Alfred told the workers that his companions had become too exhausted to continue, that he had snow blindness and frostbite, and that he had been left behind to fend for himself. Alfred said that for months he had eaten rabbits, roots, and rosebuds before getting out alive. The agency’s workers found it strange that Alfred looked well fed. By May, when Preston Nutter arrived at the agency as the leader of the party that had followed the river, Alfred had already arrived alone and left again; none of the other men had been with him. Alfred later went to Saguache, rented a room and saloon, spent over $100 on drinking and gambling, and spent another $78 in a general store. When he was drinking, Alfred often gave conflicting stories about what had happened. Some people said he seemed to use a different wallet each time he went out and never appeared to run out of cash. Alfred had sold his rifle at the agency for only $10, which did not explain the rest of the money. Preston went to Saguache and became immediately suspicious of Alfred’s story. He told General Adams that the other men would not have left Alfred for dead. Preston said the rifle Alfred sold belonged to an old man in the group and that the pipe Alfred left behind belonged to Shannon Bell. He also pointed out that Alfred had no money when he first joined the group. General Adams sent a man on horseback to bring Alfred in for questioning. When Alfred returned, Adams and his men asked where he got the money, why he had the other men’s belongings, and how he had survived the mountains while appearing well fed. Alfred first claimed that he had stayed by the fire after getting his feet wet and cold while the others went for food. He said that when the others did not return, he assumed they had abandoned him. The source says that, because the account still made no sense to Preston, a council was formed to investigate the matter further.

As the meeting began, two Ute men arrived with pieces of flesh they said came from a human found on a hill near the agency. The account says Alfred panicked, fainted, woke up, begged for mercy, and then, sobbing, gave a different story. Alfred was reportedly heard to say, “It would not be the first time that people had been obliged to eat each other when they were hungry.” He then said that ten days into the journey the party ran out of food. According to Alfred, the oldest man died first, and the others ate him and took his rifle. Five days later, another man died, and the group ate him too; Alfred said they found $133 in that man’s pockets. Alfred said another man later died while he was gathering wood for the fire, and, according to Alfred, the remaining men ate that man as well. Alfred said Shannon Bell then shot the remaining men. He said that he and Shannon carried some of the bodies for food and covered up the rest. Alfred said Shannon later tried to kill him, and that he shot Shannon in self-defense. General Adams wrote down Alfred’s confession and made him sign it as a sworn statement. Preston did not believe Alfred and thought Alfred had killed the others and stolen their belongings. Preston became so angry that he dragged Alfred outside and would have killed him if others had not intervened.

File: The bodies and investigation

single source

The account says Alfred was arrested for manslaughter and locked in a log cabin owned by the sheriff of Saguache. That summer, General Adams took Alfred and some men into the mountains to search for the bodies, but they found nothing. In August, while Alfred was awaiting trial, illustrator John Randolph was traveling over the mountains near Lake City. Near a tributary of the Gunnison River, close to where Alfred had said he left Shannon, John noticed something sticking out of the ground. He found five men in different states of decomposition, and it was clear they had died violently. One man was little more than bones, apparently after animals had gotten to him. Two men had blunt-force injuries to the head, and Shannon Bell had been stripped to the bones except for his hands and feet and also had a blunt head injury. The remains showed a deliberate removal of the edible portions; with the exception of the first man, it did not look as though animals had done it. John made a sketch and reported the scene to authorities in Lake City, after which a team of 20 volunteers recovered the bodies. The coroner concluded that they had all been killed by blows to the head while asleep. None of the bodies had defensive wounds or injuries, and they all had similar skull markings. The bodies had rags under their feet, suggesting they may have eaten the leather from their shoes, and authorities also found a track to a makeshift shelter. These findings led people to speculate that Alfred had killed the men for their possessions, become trapped by weather, and eaten them to survive. Alfred’s charges were expected to be upgraded from manslaughter to first-degree murder, but before that could happen, someone gave him a key, a penknife, and some food so he could escape. The account says that, over the following century, several groups conducted forensic analyses of the remains and compared them with Alfred’s account. Their conclusions have tended to lean toward Alfred being guilty, although some analyses found defensive wounds on some of the bones in the group. One group found marks across Shannon Bell’s forearms, suggesting that Shannon may have defended himself from an attack. In Alfred’s account, however, Shannon was only shot once and then finished quickly. Some evidence also seems to corroborate Alfred’s story: an 1862 Colt revolver found at the murder site in 1994 was still loaded with three .38-caliber bullets, and those bullets matched lead fragments found in Shannon Bell’s hip. That match suggests that at least part of Alfred’s story may have been true.
